findings.title: New refresh code uses prisma without importing it
findings.body: The newly added refresh block calls `prisma.credential.update(...)`, but this file has no `prisma` import (imports are jsforce, rrule, zod, CalEventParser, constants, HttpError, logger, types and getAppKeysFromSlug). Every Salesforce client construction will fail type-checking / throw ReferenceError at runtime before a connection can be created, breaking the integration entirely, not only when credential sync is enabled.

findings.title: Refreshed Salesforce access token is discarded and stale token is used
findings.body: getClient fetches and persists `accessTokenParsed.data`, but then constructs the jsforce Connection with `accessToken: credentialKey.access_token` (the old credential key) and `instanceUrl: credentialKey.instance_url`. After an expiry-driven refresh the client therefore continues calling Salesforce with the expired token, so the new refresh logic does not actually fix/perform authenticated calls.

findings.title: SafeParse result object is stored as the Google credential key
findings.body: `parseRefreshTokenResponse` returns the Zod SafeParse result (`{success, data}`), whereas the previous code stored `googleCredentialSchema.parse(googleCredentials)` (the credential object itself). This line stores that wrapper as `key` in prisma.credential.update. The persisted key no longer has top-level access_token/refresh_token/expiry_date, so subsequent `googleCredentialSchema.parse(credential.key)` calls fail and the user's Google credential is corrupted.

findings.title: Missing refresh_token is replaced with the literal string "refresh_token"
findings.body: When the (sync) token response has no refresh_token, this mutates the parsed data to `refresh_token = "refresh_token"`. Callers such as Zoom and Office365 then copy that value into the stored credential (`key.refresh_token = newTokens.refresh_token` / spreading tokenResponse.data), permanently overwriting the real refresh token with a placeholder. The next refresh will fail with invalid_grant and the user must reconnect; the correct behaviour is to preserve the existing stored refresh token.

findings.title: Minimum sync schema strips all fields except access_token
findings.body: The computed keys `[z.string().toString()]` and `[z.string().optional().toString()]` do not express wildcard/ passthrough fields in Zod; a plain z.object strips unknown keys by default. In sync mode the returned data therefore contains essentially only access_token (plus the fabricated refresh_token), losing expires_in/expiry_date, token_type, scope and provider-specific fields. Zoom then computes `expiry_date = Date.now() + undefined*1000` (NaN) and Office365 never updates its transformed expiry, causing broken expiry handling and repeated/invalid refreshes.

findings.title: Sync branch returns a fetch Response incompatible with non-fetch callers
findings.body: When sync is enabled this returns the raw `fetch` Response, but several wrapped refresh functions do not return a Response: HubSpot returns a HubspotToken object, Zoho CRM/Bigin return AxiosResponses with `.data`, and Google's wrapper returns `fetchTokens.res`. Callers then read properties like `.accessToken`, `.expiresIn` or `.data.error`/`.data.access_token` directly off the Response, getting undefined (and NaN expiry in HubSpot) or throwing. The sync path is therefore broken for those apps while the non-sync path works, because the helper changes the return-type contract based on an env flag.

findings.title: Credential ID is passed where refreshOAuthTokens expects a user ID
findings.body: refreshOAuthTokens' third argument is `userId` and is sent to the sync endpoint as `calcomUserId`; every other caller passes `credential.userId`. This caller passes `credentialId` (the credential row id, captured as credentialId in biginAuth). The parent platform will look up tokens for the wrong user (or a non-existent user), returning wrong/no tokens, and team credentials would incorrectly be treated as user credentials.

findings.title: Webhook secret is compared with non-constant-time string equality
findings.body: The shared secret that alone authorizes creating/updating arbitrary users' third-party credentials is checked with `!==` against the header value. This is subject to timing side-channels and, because there is no method restriction or try/catch around the subsequent `schema.parse` (line 31) and `symmetricDecrypt`/`JSON.parse` (lines 57-59), malformed unauthenticated-adjacent requests also produce unhandled 500s. Use a timing-safe comparison (with length handling) and return 400 for parse/decrypt failures instead of leaking stack-level 500 errors.
